answer.text: React too strongly to new info, pushing prices too far

explanation.text: The Logic: "Overreaction" in behavioural finance describes the empirical tendency of investors to react too strongly to new information — particularly dramatic or salient news — driving asset prices above or below their fundamental values in the short run. Subsequent mean reversion as prices correct is the symptom that distinguishes overreaction from a rational, proportionate response to information. The Trap: "Ignore new info" describes underreaction, the opposite phenomenon, where investors update their beliefs too slowly. "Always react correctly" and "never react" describe idealised or null behaviour that is inconsistent with documented investor behaviour. Only "react too strongly to new info, pushing prices too far" captures the overreaction definition. Note: The cited pages of the NISM-Series-XXI-B Portfolio Managers workbook (around p.236-p.247) discuss anomalies, systematic mistakes, momentum and behavioural biases but do not explicitly define "overreaction" or state that investors react too strongly to new information and push prices too far. The framing above is general behavioural-finance knowledge.
